common_name: Fay's Prolific Currant (Historic American Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring into fertile, cool, moisture-retentive soil; space plants to allow good air movement since the variety's heavy fruit clusters benefit from airflow to limit mildew.

directions: Fay's Prolific is a nineteenth-century American red currant raised by George Fay of Chautauqua County, New York, and for decades it was considered one of the largest-fruited and heaviest-cropping red currants in commerce. It carries its very large, bright red berries on long, well-filled strigs, though the wood is somewhat more brittle than other red currants and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind. Because it needs real winter chill and cool summer nights to perform well, it is best treated as a cool-climate specialty planting rather than a dependable crop in hot, humid regions. Fay's Prolific was also an important parent in later American currant breeding, contributing its large fruit size to twentieth-century introductions such as Perfection.

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring in fertile, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil; provide afternoon shade in warmer climates to protect ripening fruit from scorching.

directions: Cherry is a long-cultivated French red currant dating to the mid-1800s, grown for its very large, glossy, deep-red berries borne in short, tightly packed clusters rather than the long strigs typical of many other red currant cultivars. The flavor is tart and robust even at full ripeness, making Cherry better suited to jelly, syrup, and baking than fresh eating. Like most European red currants it needs substantial winter chill and cool summer nights to crop well, so it performs poorly in hot, mild-winter climates. Cherry became historically significant as a parent cultivar, crossed with Fay's Prolific to produce the widely grown American currant Perfection in the early twentieth century.

common_name: Gloire de Sablons Currant (Historic French Pink Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring in cool, fertile, moisture-retentive soil; mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

directions: Gloire de Sablons is an old French currant cultivar grown for its translucent, blush pink-rose berries, a naturally occurring color break from standard red currant valued for its milder, sweeter flavor and striking appearance on the strig. The bush is self-fertile and crops reliably on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood, requiring only light annual renewal pruning rather than hard cutting back. Its pale, jewel-toned clusters make it a favorite for garnishing desserts and for fresh eating by gardeners who find standard red currants too tart. Like other pink and red currants, it needs a genuine winter chill period and performs best in cool-summer regions.

common_name: Calhoun Sweet Watermelon (Louisiana Heirloom Parent of Calhoun Gray)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 70°F; give vines ample room since Calhoun Sweet is a full-sized vining type.

directions: Calhoun Sweet is a Louisiana watermelon strain grown and selected at the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station for exceptionally high sugar content, producing oblong, light green-rinded fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. On its own the strain carries limited resistance to the fungal wilts that plague Southern watermelon patches, which is why breeders crossed it with the disease-tolerant Charleston Gray to create the widely grown Calhoun Gray in 1965. Grown today mainly by heirloom seed savers and regional variety trial programs rather than commercial growers, it remains of interest as the sweetness parent behind one of the Deep South's standard disease-resistant watermelons. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars.

common_name: Ruhm von Braunschweig Asparagus (Glory of Brunswick, Historic German Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant one- or two-year crowns in trenches enriched with well-rotted manure as soon as the soil can be worked; this older open-pollinated strain is dioecious, so expect both male and female plants in the bed.

directions: Ruhm von Braunschweig ('Glory of Brunswick') is a nineteenth-century German open-pollinated asparagus that became one of the standard garden and market strains across Central Europe for generations before modern all-male hybrids took over commercial production. It produces thick, well-flavored green spears on a vigorous, dioecious planting, with female plants setting red berries that can self-sow into a weedy stand if left uncollected each fall. Because every seedling varies slightly, older beds grown from this strain show more variation in spear thickness and timing than named hybrid crowns, which breeders prized as useful raw material for more uniform supermale lines. It remains historically important as a direct ancestor of modern Dutch all-male hybrids such as Franklim, bred from a supermale line developed through self-pollination of this very cultivar.

planting.note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or container plants in early spring after the last frost; provide a sturdy T-trellis at planting since canes still reach 8-10 feet despite the lack of thorns.

directions: LY59 is the standard thornless strain of loganberry grown in home gardens, selected as a spineless sport of the original thorny loganberry discovered in California in the 1880s. It carries the same long, dark red, tart-sweet fruit and vigorous trailing growth as the thorny original, but the absence of spines makes training canes onto a trellis and picking the fruit far more comfortable. Train new primocanes along the wires through summer, separate from the current year's fruiting canes, then cut all spent fruiting canes to the ground after harvest and tie in the new growth for the following year. In borderline zones, lay the flexible canes down and mulch over them after leaf drop for winter protection.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; this hybrid tolerates garden conditions somewhat better than pure nagoonberry but still needs cool summers to thrive.

directions: Mespi is a Finnish-bred interspecific hybrid between nagoonberry (Rubus arcticus) and the related Alaskan species Rubus stellatus, developed to combine the nagoonberry's intensely fragrant, rich flavor with improved vigor, yield, and berry size over the wild species. Like its nagoonberry parent, it spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a low, rose-flowered groundcover, but it sets a heavier crop of small, deep rose-red berries over a longer harvest window. It still requires cool, moist, acidic growing conditions and struggles outside short-summer, cold-winter climates, making it unsuitable much south of zone 5 or 6 except at high elevation. Divide rhizomes in early spring to establish new plantings, and keep the bed consistently moist through the growing season.
